# Final independent retrieval answers

Each task uses only its named package. These are proposed actions, not executed builds, fixes or releases.

## Task A: kmp-ios-integration

### (1) Pod-based app builds locally but Gradle cannot find pod; repair plan?

Inspect the Gemfile/lockfile, Ruby manager and working pod executable and compare with Gradle's resolution. Preserve the project's pinned bundle/toolchain. Point kotlin.apple.cocoapods.bin in local.properties to the actual working executable; the reference's rbenv path is an example. Verify resolution and use podInstall for the configured Podfile, while respecting existing Bundler or multi-project commands. Open .xcworkspace and build the actual scheme/configuration. Avoid global Ruby replacement or broad gem updates. If logs identify sandboxing, disable User Script Sandboxing and stop a daemon that started sandboxed. Report the integration route, generated module and observed build results. No blocking package ambiguity remains.

### (2) A Swift consumer cancels a suspend call and stops a Flow; how to establish behavior?

Inspect Kotlin version and selected bridge, including caller-thread restrictions for that version/configuration. Default Objective-C interop provides basic async/completion handlers without proper cancellation and opaque Flow objects. Preserve existing SKIE, KMP-NativeCoroutines or explicit bridge and avoid overlapping transformations. Compile a Swift consumer importing the actual generated module, then exercise cancellation of the suspending call and termination of Flow consumption. Observe both Swift termination and Kotlin work/resource cleanup, alongside success/error paths. A Kotlin compile does not establish the behavior. The package supplies the verification target; the existing app's bridge determines the implementation. No blocking ambiguity remains.

### (3) A throwing exported function crashes Swift; what change/verification?

Identify the export path and thrown exception. For Objective-C export declare expected handleable exception types with @Throws, preferring specific types; unexpected exceptions crossing the boundary still terminate the process. Build the actual Xcode scheme and compile a Swift caller against the generated module. Exercise normal success and declared errors with Swift error handling, and cancellation if the API suspends. Verify actual generated spelling and observed runtime behavior. No blocking ambiguity remains.

### (4) Existing production ObjC framework works; does this skill mandate Swift export adoption, and what would be needed to try it?

No. Preserve the production Objective-C bridge. Swift export is a separate Alpha path in this package, evaluated only when explicitly requested or its capabilities are required. A trial needs the installed Kotlin release and integration capabilities checked, its distinct build integration configured, and a real Swift consumer compiled and exercised for the APIs needed, including error/cancellation/stream behavior. The reference says it supports direct integration. Do not assume Objective-C mappings or bridge behavior carry over. No blocking ambiguity remains for this adoption decision and trial plan.

## Task B: compose-multiplatform-ui

### (1) Fix a laggy embedded map inside an existing full-Compose iOS screen.

Preserve the existing full-Compose shell. Inspect CMP/Kotlin version and the affected screen, reproduce the lag and check native gesture arbitration. UIKitInteropProperties defaults to cooperative touch handling with a 150 ms delay. If the map should own touches immediately, set interactionMode = UIKitInteropInteractionMode.NonCooperative via properties = on the interop view/controller. Verify map gestures and surrounding Compose scroll behavior, including any ownership tradeoff. Judge performance on a release build on a real iOS device and record screen, OS, device and build mode. If lag persists, investigate actual rendering behavior for the installed version instead of declaring the setting a universal fix. No blocking ambiguity remains.

### (2) Native SwiftUI tabs need system navigation chrome with a pre-iOS-26 deployment target; propose ownership and compatibility approach.

Let SwiftUI own tabs and navigation; Compose renders tab roots and individual destination controllers. Bridge events in both directions, assign each event a single stack owner and hide Compose's navigation chrome. Liquid Glass requires the iOS 26 SDK/Xcode 26+ and an iOS 26 runtime. Older OS versions can retain the native shell and their normal native appearance. NavigationStack requires iOS 16; iOS 14/15 support needs an available navigation container or availability branch. Keeping a separate full-Compose shell for older releases is optional, not inherently required by pre-26 support. Verify oldest supported OS and iOS 26, back behavior, tab changes and disposal. No blocking ambiguity remains; the revised reference explicitly supplies the relevant version distinction.

### (3) Swift swipe-back leaves an extra Kotlin destination; what evidence needed?

Record Swift and Kotlin stacks before/after the gesture, callback order/direction and which layer owns the pop. Reproduce completed and cancelled swipe-back, ordinary back, tab changes, repeated navigation and deep links. Check destination disposal and whether a forwarded event was replayed into both stacks. With Navigation 3, inspect entry decorators and destination-scoped ViewModel disposal as applicable. Report device/OS/build mode and observed stack/lifecycle behavior. The reference labels its migration snippet a sketch with coordinator/state-restoration details omitted, so investigate the app's actual coordinator. This is sufficient guidance to collect the requested evidence; no blocking ambiguity remains.

### (4) Screen looks fine on Desktop but VoiceOver skips its embedded UIKit view; how verify completion?

Inspect the embedded view's own accessibility content and isNativeAccessibilityEnabled, which defaults off. Enable native accessibility for the interop view when it requires its own VoiceOver support. Verify on iOS with VoiceOver that labels, actions and focus order work across the native/Compose boundary. Use testTag/accessibilityIdentifier in XCTest and accessibility audits where supported. Do not restore the removed AccessibilitySyncOptions knob; the package states synchronization is automatic since 1.8. Report screen, device/OS/build mode and observed behavior. Desktop appearance alone is insufficient. No blocking ambiguity remains.

## Task C: kmp-release-and-publish

### (1) User asks prepare release artifacts but gives no upload request; what actions/results?

Identify deliverables and inspect existing release configuration and pipeline. Build/validate the requested local artifacts: actual signed/minified Android variant and relevant smoke tests; actual iOS archive with framework/resources/privacy coverage and matching symbols; or library coordinates/version/tag/metadata/signing/target artifacts. Preserve existing secret handling and distribution method. Report artifact paths, platform/variant and verification results, with upload/publication status separately stated as not performed. Preparation authorizes neither external staging nor test-track/public upload. Before a subsequently authorized external action identify exact version, artifact and destination. No blocking ambiguity remains.

### (2) Library needs SNAPSHOT distribution to testers using Central Portal; what path?

Enable snapshots for the namespace, publish a -SNAPSHOT version through the separate Central Portal snapshot endpoint and configure testers to opt into that repository. Inspect the installed publishing plugin and task/help output for the precise commands, use a Portal user token and protected secret bindings, and validate intended publications/metadata with one coordinated publisher. Snapshots do not follow the immutable release contract. Check automatic-release configuration instead of inferring authorization boundaries from task names. The reference provides the specific Sonatype snapshot guide and installed-plugin guidance, which are enough to direct implementation; no blocking ambiguity remains for the requested path. Exact commands require the project/plugin, not a universal package recipe.

### (3) Upload timed out and we do not know if deployment exists; next action?

Inspect remote deployment/artifact state for the exact version and destination before retrying. Resume an existing deployment where supported. If destination/version or status cannot be established, stop and report uncertainty rather than blindly repeating an immutable release. Report upload status separately from public-release status. No blocking ambiguity remains for this next-action decision.

### (4) Pure Apple klibs plus Android have no cinterop today; is macOS always mandatory, and what changes with an iOS app archive/static shared framework symbols?

No. Pure Apple klibs can be produced on other hosts in supported configurations. Derive runners from actual tasks and installed toolchain; Android checks can run on Linux. A coordinated macOS publisher is a simple option, not a universal requirement. Apple binary linking, simulator tests and Xcode archives need macOS, while CocoaPods/cinterop introduce additional host constraints. When archiving an iOS app, inspect actual scheme/configuration, device architecture, linkage and matching symbols. Static shared code lands in the app binary, so inspect the archive's matching symbol files rather than assuming an independently uploaded shared-framework dSYM exists. No blocking ambiguity remains.

## Result and limitations

All 12 questions can be answered with an actionable plan or decision using their respective package. No remaining ambiguity prevents carrying out the requested task. The earlier CocoaPods quick-path inconsistency, native-shell SDK/runtime scope, native navigation availability gap and caller-thread overgeneralization are resolved in the revised text.

No application or pipeline was inspected, no linked external documentation was opened, and no builds, runtime tests, uploads or releases occurred. This validates retrieval and steering, not observed application correctness or third-party API accuracy. Project-specific code and provider commands remain normal implementation inputs, not package blockers. Final consulted paths, SHA256 values, timestamp and known model identity are in metadata.json.
